summary: Extends Kerberos so a client can talk to a service without revealing its identity, or only its realm, and can get anonymous credentials from the key distribution center. It updates earlier Kerberos RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: Like entering a club with a pass that proves you belong without saying your name.

questions: how to get an anonymous kerberos ticket
what is the kerberos anonymous realm
subtitle: How a Kerberos client can prove who a server is without telling the server, or even the KDC, who the client is.

tldr.problem: A Kerberos client sometimes wants to authenticate a service and protect its traffic without revealing its own identity, for example when querying a research database open to arbitrary requesters.
tldr.mechanism: The client sets a new anonymous KDC option to get an anonymous ticket, either by authenticating normally or by using anonymous PKINIT, which hides the identity from the KDC too.
tldr.outcome: This document obsoletes RFC 6112, which contained errors and did not interoperate with any known implementation, and describes a protocol that interoperates with multiple implementations.

today: RFC 8062 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 6112, which it reclassifies as Historic, and it updates RFC 4120, RFC 4121 and RFC 4556. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Anonymity in Kerberos
sections.content:
In Kerberos, a client normally proves who it is. Sometimes a client only wants to authenticate the server and protect the conversation, without disclosing its own identity. The RFC's example is an application that gives read access to a research database and allows queries by arbitrary requesters: the client wants to trust the answers but has privacy reasons not to reveal who it is.

The RFC defines extensions so a client can authenticate the Key Distribution Center (KDC) and request an anonymous ticket. The client may reveal its identity to its own KDC, or hide it completely using anonymous PKINIT. Either way, it stays anonymous to KDCs on the cross-realm path and to the server.

This document replaces RFC 6112 to correct technical errors. RFC 6112 is classified as Historic and implementing it is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want to ask a library a question without giving your name. This lets you do that and still be sure you are talking to the real library.

sections.title: The Anonymous Ticket and Its Names
sections.content:
The RFC builds on the well-known names of RFC 6111. The anonymous realm is the literal WELLKNOWN:ANONYMOUS. The anonymous principal has name-type KRB_NT_WELLKNOWN and two name components, WELLKNOWN and ANONYMOUS.

Two new bits are defined, both bit 16 (counting the first bit as bit 0): an anonymous ticket flag in TicketFlags and an anonymous KDC option in KDCOptions. The option asks for an anonymous ticket; the flag marks a ticket as one.

An anonymous ticket has the anonymous principal in cname, either the client's real realm or the anonymous realm in crealm, and the flag set. It must contain nothing that reveals the client's identity. It may still carry the client realm, intermediate realms and authorization data. For example, authorization data could show that the client belongs to some group of users.
sections.plainLanguage: The pass says "Visitor" instead of your name, and it has a special stamp so everyone can tell it is an anonymous pass.

sections.title: Getting an Anonymous Ticket
sections.content:
In an AS exchange, the client sets the anonymous KDC option. It may authenticate with its long-term keys, X.509 certificates or other pre-authentication data, in which case the KDC knows who it is and the returned ticket has the realm of the AS. If the request names the anonymous principal, the option MUST be set, otherwise the KDC MUST return KDC_ERR_BADOPTION. If the KDC has no key to encrypt the reply, it MUST return KDC_ERR_NULL_KEY.

In a TGS exchange, the client sets the option and presents a normal TGT, an anonymous TGT or an anonymous cross-realm TGT. With a normal TGT the TGS learns the client's identity. If the TGT is anonymous, the option SHOULD be set. The returned ticket copies the name and realm from an anonymous ticket, or uses the anonymous principal with the client's true realm when the presented ticket was normal.

In both exchanges the realm field in the KDC request is the realm of the target KDC, not the anonymous realm. The KDC MUST NOT put any identifier in the ticket that could reveal the client to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand the ticket office a form saying "make my pass anonymous". The office checks the form and stamps a pass that has no name on it.

sections.title: Anonymous PKINIT
sections.content:
To hide its identity even from the KDC, the client uses anonymous PKINIT. It sets the client name to the anonymous principal and sends PA_PK_AS_REQ pre-authentication data whose signerInfos is empty and whose certificates field is absent. With no key pair of its own, the client MUST choose Diffie-Hellman key agreement. The ticket's realm MUST be the anonymous realm, and this is the only way in this specification to get an anonymous ticket with the anonymous realm.

The KDC skips the checks of the client's signature and public key but performs the others, such as checking the Diffie-Hellman parameters. If clientPublicValue is missing, it MUST return KDC_ERR_PUBLIC_KEY_ENCRYPTION_NOT_SUPPORTED. A KDC with no asymmetric key pair MAY reply anonymously or refuse. If its reply is anonymous (no signature), the client MUST reject the ticket unless it can authenticate the KDC some other way.

A KDC supporting anonymous PKINIT MUST indicate PKINIT support and MUST add an empty PA_PKINIT_KX padata element when it includes PA-PK-AS-REQ in an error reply.
sections.plainLanguage: You show up wearing a mask and a code you made up on the spot. The office cannot know who you are, but you can still agree on a secret with them, and you check it is really the office.

sections.title: Joint Session Key from PKINIT
sections.content:
Anonymous PKINIT needs to build secure channels, so neither side may pick the ticket session key alone. The KDC generates a random KDC contribution key and encrypts it in PA_PKINIT_KX (padata type 147) using the reply key, with key usage number KEY_USAGE_PA_PKINIT_KX (44). The ticket session key is then the combination of the contribution key and the reply key using KRB-FX-CF2, with pepper strings PKINIT and KEYEXCHANGE.

PA_PKINIT_KX MUST be included when anonymous PKINIT is used, SHOULD be included for Diffie-Hellman PKINIT with a non-anonymous client, and MUST NOT be included otherwise. A conforming client MUST reject anonymous PKINIT if it is missing or if the session key is not the combined key.

The reason given is a man-in-the-middle attack. Without this binding, an attacker could run separate Diffie-Hellman exchanges with the client and the KDC, decrypt the ticket and session key, re-encrypt them for the client and keep a copy. KRB-FX-CF2 XORs two PRF+ outputs, each built from a one-octet counter and the pseudo-random function of the key's encryption type.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one person choosing the secret code, both of you add a piece. Then a sneaky person in the middle cannot swap the code for their own.

sections.title: Client Checks and GSS-API
sections.content:
Conforming implementations MUST support the anonymous principal with a non-anonymous realm and MAY support it with the anonymous realm via anonymous PKINIT.

Because KDCs ignore unknown KDC options, a KDC that does not understand the anonymous option returns a normal ticket without an error. Unless anonymous PKINIT is used, a client that needs anonymity MUST check that the anonymous flag is set in the EncKDCRepPart.

In GSS-API, the anonymous principal with the anonymous realm matches the GSS-API anonymous identity (GSS_C_NT_ANONYMOUS). A principal with the anonymous name but a real realm is an authenticated principal and does not. A client requests anonymity by asserting the anonymous flag in GSS_Init_Sec_Context(). If anonymity turns out to be unavailable, the initiator MUST NOT send the initial token, since that would likely reveal its identity.
sections.plainLanguage: Always look at your pass before you walk in. If it has no anonymous stamp, stop, because the guard may already know your name.

sections.title: Limits of the Anonymity
sections.content:
The client stays hidden from the server, but its identity may be revealed to the KDC of the server principal when that is in a different realm, and to any KDC on the cross-realm path. The client MUST verify the ticket really is anonymous before talking to the server.

The RFC lists ways anonymity can leak. A KDC that records which identity got which ticket could breach it. KDCs reply as requests arrive, so traffic analysis can match clients to tickets, and plaintext ticket parts on the wire make this easy for an observer. A service may link requests by IP address or by reuse of the same ticket.

Mitigations include the FAST hide-client-names option of RFC 6113, Kerberos over TLS as in RFC 6251, transport or network-layer security, and limiting ticket reuse. Servers MUST avoid accepting anonymous credentials where they must record the client's identity, such as for an audit trail.
sections.plainLanguage: A pass hides your name, but people can still notice your face, where you came from, or that you use the same pass every day.
